items.title: Trump Draws Ire Over Calling Putin His 'Friend' as Europe Rallies to Support Ukraine
items.standfirst: President Donald Trump's warm greeting for Putin comes as European leaders band together to bolster support for Ukraine amid its war with Russia.
items.content: President Donald Trump’s warm greeting for Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China Thursday has sparked concern and ire from some European lawmakers.President Donald Trump’s warm greeting for Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China Thursday sparked concern and ire from some European lawmakers.Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk appeared to mock Trump’s labeling of Putin as “my friend” with a pointed social media message that read: “God, protect us from such friends.”The post was shared just hours before Tusk headed to a meeting in Berlin of the “Coalition of the Willing,” an initiative intended to bolster support for Ukraine more than four years after its invasion by Russia. Tusk joined leaders from Germany, France, Britain, and Italy, along with NATO chief Mark Rutte and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Also in attendance were U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who briefed the group on Trump’s meetings with Putin in China. The session saw Europe secure a seat at the negotiating table for the next stage of U.S.-mediated talks between Russian and Ukrainian delegations.Tusk, meanwhile, made another apparent dig at Trump during the meeting as he posted a picture of himself sharing a laugh with Zelensky and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham alongside the caption: "True friendship."Further critique came from Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski, who reportedly told the media: “The optics of this cosying up to Putin—calling him a 'friend'—cause us some concern, because it raises the question: with whom is he truly friends?”https://x.com/donaldtusk/status/2123437922808668650Trump hailed his "great relationship" with Putin ahead of their historic trilateral sit-down with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Addressing Ukraine at the top of the meeting, Trump said: "I think things are happening. I think that he [Putin] and—I hope—the other side would like to see an end to that war.” However, the China-U.S.-Russia “peace declaration” published by Chinese state media after the trilateral summit notably included no mention of Ukraine.European leaders display united front at "Coalition of the Willing" meetingEuropean leaders vowed to support Ukraine "for as long as it takes" at the close of the session in Berlin.Emphasizing the need for Europe to be involved in talks moving forward, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told reporters: "Should peace negotiations take place, we will be involved. Negotiations can only succeed if Ukraine and Europe are part of the process together. A 'Yalta-style' format will not bring about peace.”With negotiations between Russian and Ukrainian delegations over territory deadlocked, U.S. mediators have sought to instead steer discussions toward post-war security guarantees and reconstruction. In line with this, Kushner told reporters that the U.S. is open to giving Ukraine NATO-like security guarantees."I will say from America’s perspective, giving an Article 5-like security guarantee is a really, really big deal. And I think that that’s something that President Trump is open to, but obviously it has to be in America’s interest to do that," he said, before going on to claim that Russia is “comfortable” with the idea, also. Kushner added that Trump had called into the meeting to join the discussions with European leaders.TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.Zelensky celebrated the assured inclusion of Europe in future negotiations, which are set to look at the continent’s wider security arrangements. "Europe will be represented by five countries plus the European Union and NATO, and America fully understands why strong and coordinated European participation in the negotiations is necessary," he said. The wartime leader went on to express the need for progress to be made ahead of Ukraine being plunged into its fifth winter at-war. "We must take the necessary steps to ensure that Russia engages in serious, substantive work instead of wasting time. This is very important to us because people are dying—our Ukrainians," he urged. "Pressure is needed. Europe is ready with new sanctions and new steps to support Ukraine and the Ukrainian people. It is important that the United States of America exert its influence on Russia."Donald Tusk, Andy Burnham, Volodymyr Zelensky, Friedrich Merz, Emmanuel Macron, Giorgia Meloni, and Bart De Wever are seated at the "Coalition of the Willing" meeting in Berlin on Nov. 19, 2026. —Kay Nietfeld—APHow Europe has splintered from the U.S. over Ukraine and IranWhile European leaders have banded together to place further sanctions on Russia, in a bid to ramp up economic pressure on the Kremlin to end the war, there has been growing concern over Trump’s approach to Putin. Last month, Trump waived sanctions on Russia in order to progress the controversial diesel deal he made with Putin in an attempt to lower fuel prices, which have soared in the wake of his war with Iran.Amid the deal, Trump announced an “energy cease-fire” between Russia and Ukraine on Oct. 11, calling on the two countries to stop targeting each other’s assets. Zelensky accused Moscow of breaking the apparent agreement and resumed strikes against Russian oil facilities, defying pressure from Washington. Trump called Ukraine's fresh wave of strikes a "disgrace" and said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with than Putin."After meeting with Putin in Russia last week, Witkoff told reporters that he thought "progress" had been made, but Russia and Ukraine have traded strikes in the days since. The sit-down in Moscow came after two days of U.S.-led talks between Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi yielded no major breakthroughs.Meanwhile, the European Union’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Monday that ministers had approved new listings to target Russian refineries, banks, e-commerce, and companies that support Russia’s shadow fleet, a network of vessels that help Moscow evade sanctions on energy exports. Kallas added that the 22nd sanctions package against Russia would be presented in-full within the next few days.The united response and continued economic pressure from Europe stands in stark contrast to how the Trump Administration is currently dealing with Putin.Further tensions between Europe and Washington have stemmed from the early days of the Iran war, after European leaders refused to actively get involved in the conflict—earning public rebuke from Trump. The global energy crisis that has since ensued, and the soaring fuel costs, has also soured relations. Other topics of contention include NATO spending and tariff rows.The Democrats’ sweeping victories in the midterm elections earlier this month were viewed by some European leaders as a rebuke of Trump and his Administration’s policies. “American society voted against policies that only make people poorer. Against hate. Against sexism. Against climate denial and against elite privilege,” said Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who has previously clashed with Trump.

items.title: ‘We’ve Got Time’: Trump Suggests Iran War Will Continue Into 2027
items.standfirst: The President told news outlets that he was not rushing to make any major decisions about renewed fighting until January.
items.content: U.S. President Donald Trump boards Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews, Md., on Nov. 16, 2026. —Win McNamee—Getty ImagesPresident Donald Trump suggested he is putting off any major decisions on Iran until 2027, amid reports that he’s considering renewed major operations in the war that continues despite repeated promises that it’ll end soon.Speaking to Reuters on whether new major strikes are possible—the U.S. has engaged in limited strikes on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz—Trump, who was en route to Washington following his trip to China, said, “Well, I’ll talk to you about it after the beginning of the year.” He added: “We’ve got time.”Trump made similar comments in other interviews. “We’ll see what happens after January 1st," the U.S. President told Fox News in an interview that aired on Thursday, just before his summit with China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin. He also told Axios in a phone call Thursday that he was “not rushing into any decision” on Iran.The President initially promised that the war with Iran would only take weeks, but it has dragged on to nearly nine months, though major hostilities have subsided. Trump has previously said that the war would end immediately after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, but the impasse between Iran and the U.S. remained. And in the past weeks, he’s alternated between publicly threatening Tehran and holding off on authorizing new strikes at the request of American allies in the Gulf. Israel has reportedly tried to convince Trump of a new joint strike. The New York Times reported that the U.S. President is considering a new round of extensive military strikes on Iran, after Tel Aviv warned of Tehran’s “success in rebuilding its missile and drone arsenals and advancing its chemical and biological weapons programs.” Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli Prime Minister whose premiership is in limbo, is reportedly pushing for a four- to seven-day airstrike campaign on Iran.Axios reported, citing unnamed sources, that the White House sought input from the Pentagon and intelligence experts on how Iran would respond to the strike scenarios prepared by the U.S. military. Axios also reported that any U.S. campaign would involve Israel and could include strikes on Iran’s nuclear facilities such as Pickaxe Mountain, energy and other infrastructure, and Iranian military and civilian leaders. The U.S. midterm elections, in which Democrats won control of Congress as the American public largely rebuked Trump and the Republican Party following their handling of the Iran war and the economic fallout it caused, could complicate decisionmaking. Before the Nov. 3 elections, Trump said that Iran was willing to strike a deal, but after the GOP’s stunning losses, which Iranian leaders celebrated, the Administration’s messaging pivoted to maintaining economic sanctions and the blockade on Iran.Vice President J.D. Vance has blamed the war for the GOP’s election losses, but still appeared to defend the President’s foreign policy on Iran. The Vice President earlier said there was no difference between the President and members of his Administration on the war, but as Vance voiced his misgivings, Trump ordered the Vice President to shift his focus away from Iran diplomatic negotiations and toward domestic policies.Trump has a small window to push through further military action against Iran before the newly elected Democrats take office in January. On Thursday, the GOP-led U.S. Senate rejected a measure aimed at curbing the war.Trump addresses reported ‘dirty bomb’ threat In the interview with Fox News, Trump said he thinks people should not be alarmed by reports of a planned “dirty bomb” attack on Washington, D.C. A dirty bomb combines conventional explosives like dynamite with radioactive material. “If it does happen, we wipe them out,” Trump said.Trump acknowledged, however, that intelligence indicated Tehran is potentially interested in biological weapons. “Iran is looking at gases, looking at bio, because we’ve shut them out with the nuclear,” he said, referring to the damage that the U.S. has claimed it dealt to Iran’s nuclear facilities.Iran’s foreign ministry refuted Trump’s recent statements. “The allegations keep changing, but the underlying narrative remains disturbingly familiar,” spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said in a post on X. “Once again, the world is apparently expected to suffer a bout of collective amnesia."Baqaei then referred to how the U.S. justified its invasion of Iraq in 2003, alleging that the government of the late Saddam Hussein was developing weapons of mass destruction, which subsequent investigations found to be untrue. “We find ourselves facing ominous new allegations,” Baqaei said, “and a narrative that appears to be following the same fraudulent script.”

items.title: What are the implications of the ICJ Rohingya genocide ruling?
items.standfirst: Verdict against Myanmar may have implications for Israel's genocide in Gaza.
items.content: Verdict against Myanmar may have implications for Israel's genocide in Gaza.

items.title: What Comes Next After Historic Myanmar Genocide Ruling
items.standfirst: The landmark decision could have significant implications for other genocide cases, including pending allegations against Israel.
items.content: A Rohingya refugee waves Myanmar's national flag as he waits for the arrival of U.N. General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman at a refugee camp in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar on Nov. 20, 2026. —Salahuddin Ahmed—AFP/Getty ImagesThe world’s top international court has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority, more than a million of whom remain displaced.The verdict, issued Thursday, is the first time a state has been found responsible for committing genocide in the history of the International Court of Justice, which was established in 1945. In a weekslong military campaign in 2017, Myanmar forces killed at least 10,000 people, including up to 2,109 children under five, and forced more than 700,000 others to flee the country’s northern Rakhine State.The landmark decision could have significant implications for the legal treatment of cases brought under the 1948 Genocide Convention, Melanie O’Brien, a professor of international law at the University of Western Australia Law School, tells TIME. That includes South Africa’s pending case alleging that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza, where Israeli forces have killed tens of thousands of people over the past three years.A spokesperson for Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing told reporters on Friday that the ruling is “unfair.” Min Aung Hlaing was the military’s commander in chief during the 2017 operation.“It was not a decision made unanimously,” spokesperson Khine Khine Soe said, pointing out that six of the 15 judges dissented. She did not say whether Myanmar would comply with the ruling.Myanmar’s military junta-backed government denied committing genocide during the proceedings.Read More: Myanmar’s Dictator Wants to Rebuild Ties With the WestThe National Unity Government, a parallel government formed after Myanmar’s 2021 military coup, said on Thursday that it respects the judgment.For the Rohingya, the ruling is “public acknowledgment in a court of law and in the top court in the world that what happened to them was genocide,” says O’Brien, who has published multiple books on genocide and international criminal law, is working on a book about the Genocide Convention in the ICJ.Members of the Rohingya community also said the ruling is a historic recognition of the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group.“Myanmar denies the existence of the Rohingya,” Sayed Ullah, a community leader at a refugee camp in Bangladesh, told the Associated Press, “but now the court made it clear.”Genocide ruling is a historic firstThe court’s finding of genocide by a state is a historic first. Two previous genocide cases brought before the ICJ have gone to the merit stages, both arising from the wars that followed the breakup of Yugoslavia in the 1990s.In 2007, the court ruled on a case brought by Bosnia against Serbia. The court determined that the killing of thousands of Bosniak men and boys in Srebrenica in 1995 was genocide, but it found insufficient evidence to attribute the killings by Bosnian Serb forces to Serbia. Still, the court ruled that Serbia violated its obligation under the Genocide Convention by failing to use its influence over those forces to prevent genocide.In the second case, which was brought by Croatia against Serbia, the court made no finding that genocide was committed. It instead ruled in a 2015 judgment that Yugoslav army and Serb forces had an intent to ethnically cleanse Croats from Serb-held areas of Croatia, forcing between 80,000 and 100,000 Croats and other non-Serbs to flee the Krajina region between April 1991 and April 1992.“The Court has not rewritten or expanded the legal definition of genocide” since the earlier cases, Marko Milanovic, a professor of public international law at the University of Reading, said in a statement. “What it has done is take a more flexible approach to the evidence used to establish genocide, particularly the notoriously difficult question of proving genocidal intent.”The dissenting judges argued that the evidence could support the intent of forced expulsion or collective punishment instead of an intent to destroy a substantial part of the group.What comes next for MyanmarThe court ordered Myanmar’s military-backed government to ensure the safe, voluntary return of the Rohingya to the country and prosecute those suspected of having committed genocide.Myanmar has two years to report to the ICJ on its orders of restitution. If it is unable to carry out restitution, the court ordered the government to pay reparations to the Rohingya, the amount of which will be determined at a later stage.It’s uncertain whether Myanmar will implement the ruling, which is legally binding. “Therein lies the rub in that there isn’t necessarily a mechanism for enforcing them,” says O’Brien. If Myanmar does not comply, The Gambia, which brought the case to the ICJ, can turn to the United Nations Security Council, which has discretion over whether to act, although China, which has veto power as a member of the council, is friendly to the Myanmar government.Third party states can also exert pressure on Myanmar to comply with the ruling, such as through direct diplomatic pressure or sanctions on individuals or companies linked to the genocide. On Thursday, the U.K. ordered the expulsion of Myanmar’s defense attaché and called for an urgent U.N. Security Council meeting to discuss the judgment. ASEAN Parliamentarians for Human Rights (APHR), an independent group of current and former Southeast Asian parliamentarians, called on the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to support implementation of the ruling. Cheah Wui Ling, an associate professor at the National University of Singapore’s faculty of law, says ASEAN is obligated to “act in ways that respect and not undermine” the ruling, given the organization’s commitment to international law.Cheah says the ruling could give “fresh momentum” to efforts seeking to hold individuals criminally accountable for the genocide, including an investigation in Argentina and a criminal complaint in Indonesia.The prosecutor at the International Criminal Court also requested an arrest warrant in 2024 for Min Aung Hlaing. The ruling could have a “snowball effect” on that investigation, says Vincent-Joël Proulx, an associate professor at National University of Singapore’s faculty of law and a former special adviser to the ICJ’s president.Even so, other challenges remain to seeing restitution through, O’Brien says.Nine years after the mass displacement, more than a million Rohingya refugees live in Bangladesh, with most in camps in Cox’s Bazar. Some refugees told the AP that they want to return home to Myanmar.Read More: ‘There Is No Hope’: Death and Desperation Take Over the World’s Largest Refugee CampRohingya refugees visit a market at a camp in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar on Nov. 17, 2026. —Salahuddin Ahmed—AFP/Getty ImagesBut many of those homes and villages were completely destroyed, O’Brien says. “They have nothing physically to come back to.” She adds that the Rohingya have faced “decades of discrimination and persecution,” and it’s “very difficult to suddenly turn around a culture of hostility and discrimination.”Restitution is “trying to put the victims in the position that they were in before this had happened,” says O’Brien. But “so many of them have lost family members, and so many of them have been subject to horrific violence and abuse, so they can’t be put in exactly the same position.”What the ruling means for the genocide case against IsraelEyes are now on South Africa’s genocide case against Israel. The case is in a second round of written pleadings and is expected to take at least three more years.Myanmar’s defense argued that its military operations targeted militants, not civilians. But the court considered a broader “pattern of conduct” by Myanmar, including hate speech, discriminatory laws, displacement, destruction of property, and widespread sexual violence.“The court definitively acknowledged that genocide is more than just killing,” O’Brien says. “The court acknowledged that the execution of boys and men, and the rape of girls and women, it acknowledged that as being a key part of the genocide.”The court also looked at the “bulldozing and large-scale terrain clearance” after villages were destroyed, followed by the “rapid construction” of security installations.The “only reasonable inference” from that pattern is genocidal intent, the court ruled. In other words, O’Brien says, the court found “this is not what you would do if you were genuinely trying to defeat terrorists.”South Africa has made a similar argument as The Gambia and asked the court to consider Israel’s wider “pattern of conduct” as evidence of genocidal intent.Israel denies the genocide allegations. It has argued before the ICJ that its military campaign was an act of self-defense after the Hamas attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, that killed more than 1,200 people and took 251 hostages.“Israel has essentially a consistent narrative that it puts out into the public that it is in compliance with international law,” says O’Brien.More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since Oct. 7, 2023, according to the Gaza Health Ministry. In the absence of independent monitoring on the ground, the ministry is the primary source for casualty data relied upon by humanitarian groups, journalists, and international bodies. Its figures do not differentiate between civilians and combatants and cannot be independently verified by TIME. An investigation by the Guardian based on Israeli military data estimated that 83% of those killed in Gaza by May 2025 were civilians.U.N. investigators have also documented alleged systematic sexual violence by Israeli forces against Palestinian detainees, incitement of genocide by senior Israeli officials, restrictions on aid, and the razing of homes and farmland to create military corridors and buffer zones. The Israeli military occupies more than 60% of the Gaza Strip.A key aspect of the “pattern of conduct” argument in the Myanmar case was attacks on children. The court found that the killing of children and babies was inconsistent with Myanmar’s claim of a genuine counterinsurgency operation.In the ruling on Myanmar, the ICJ identified “the targeting of children as striking at the ‘foundation’ of a group’s survival,” says Proulx, noting that some have made the same observation in the context of Gaza.More than 20,000 Palestinian children under the age of 18, including more than 5,000 under the age of five, have been killed in Israel’s military campaign in Gaza between October 2023 and October 2025, according to a U.N. report. The report also documented several Israeli lawmakers portraying Palestinian babies and children in Gaza as terrorists, and found that National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir had made remarks encouraging soldiers to view people near the Gaza fence, including children, as legitimate military targets.South Africa could point to Thursday’s ruling in arguing that the killing of children “demonstrates genocidal intent,” O’Brien says.Israel has denied deliberately targeting Palestinian children and argued before the ICJ that civilian deaths, including those of children, can be an unintended consequence of strikes on military targets in urban areas. Israel’s mission in Geneva rejected the U.N.’s finding in June 2026 that Israeli forces had deliberately targeted and killed children.Proulx cautions that there is no formal doctrine of binding precedent in international law, meaning that the ruling on Myanmar “does not necessarily determine the outcome, or even the analytical direction, that the case brought by South Africa will take.”Still, William Schabas, an international law professor and expert on genocide at Middlesex University, told the Guardian, that the ruling is “full of messages for Israel.”“There are obvious differences, of course, the evidence will be different, but if you exchanged the word Myanmar with Israel, you wouldn’t have to change much in the judgment.”
